title: Understand the suitability of horse breeds for designated purposes

lessons.title: Historic development of horse breeds
lessons.html:
How breeds developed

All modern horse breeds come from the domestic horse, Equus caballus. People selected horses over centuries for the work they needed: speed for war and racing, strength for farming and haulage, endurance for long journeys, and hardiness for difficult climates. Isolation and local conditions also shaped breeds. A breed is a group of horses with consistent, inherited characteristics, usually recorded in a stud book kept by a breed society.

Broad categories

CategoryTypical traitsExample breeds
Hot bloodsFine-boned, spirited, fast, high enduranceArabian, Thoroughbred
WarmbloodsCrosses of hot bloods with heavier types; athletic, trainableHanoverian, Dutch Warmblood (KWPN), Trakehner
Cold bloods (draught)Heavy, powerful, calmShire, Clydesdale, Percheron
PoniesUnder about 14.2 hands, hardy, thriftyBasuto pony, Welsh, Shetland
Stock and gaited horsesBred for ranch work or special gaitsAmerican Quarter Horse, American Saddlebred

Development of selected breeds

Arabian: developed by the Bedouin of the Arabian peninsula, selected for endurance, soundness and a close bond with people in the desert. It has influenced almost every light breed.

Thoroughbred: developed in England in the 17th and 18th centuries from native racing mares crossed with three imported Eastern foundation stallions: the Byerley Turk, the Darley Arabian and the Godolphin Arabian. Selection for racing speed has been strict ever since, and the breed is recorded in the General Stud Book.

Percheron: a French draught breed from the Perche region, used for farm work and haulage, with Arabian influence that gives it relatively free movement for a heavy horse.

American Quarter Horse: developed in colonial America for short sprint races over about a quarter of a mile, and later for cattle work on ranches.

South African breeds

  • Boerperd: descends from horses brought to the Cape from the 1650s onward by the Dutch East India Company, later mixed with other imports. It became a hardy, versatile farm and riding horse, and in recent times has been developed by breed societies.
  • Basuto pony: developed in the mountains of Lesotho from Cape horses during the 1800s. Harsh conditions selected a small, very tough, sure-footed pony.
  • Nooitgedacht: a South African breed developed in the 20th century from Basuto pony-type stock through a state breeding programme, aiming to preserve the hardiness and sure-footedness of the Basuto type.

lessons.title: Breed characteristics
lessons.html:
Describing a breed

Breed standards set out by breed societies describe the ideal type. When identifying a breed, consider:

  • Height and build (frame, bone, muscling)
  • Head shape and profile
  • Neck, back and croup shape
  • Colours permitted
  • Gaits and movement
  • Temperament
  • Hardiness and special traits

Characteristics of selected breeds

BreedKey characteristics
ArabianSmall to medium; dished (concave) face, large eyes, small ears; high tail carriage; short back; spirited and intelligent; excellent endurance
ThoroughbredTall, lean and long-legged; deep chest; fine skin and coat; long, sloping shoulder; bred for speed; sensitive, often energetic temperament
Warmblood (e.g. Hanoverian)Tall, athletic, substantial bone; powerful hindquarters; elastic movement; generally trainable temperament; bred for dressage and jumping
PercheronHeavy, muscular, usually grey or black; clean legs with little feathering; calm and willing
Quarter HorseCompact, very muscular hindquarters; short head; fast over short distances; calm; strong "cow sense"
FriesianBlack; long, thick mane and tail; feathering on the lower legs; high knee action; popular in South Africa for driving and dressage
BoerperdMedium-sized, strong and hardy; good-natured; versatile under saddle and in harness; may show additional gaits in some lines
Basuto ponySmall, stocky, tough hooves; sure-footed on rocky slopes; can thrive on poor grazing; strong endurance
NooitgedachtPony-sized to small horse; hardy, sure-footed, good hooves; calm and willing; suitable for trail and farm riding

Breed versus type

A breed is registered in a stud book with known ancestry. A type describes a body shape and use, for example a "hunter", "hack" or "cob", and may include horses of mixed breeding. When buying, always check registration papers and identity if breed matters for the purpose, for example breeding or breed shows.

Using the breed societies

South African breed societies publish breed standards, inspection rules and registered stud books. They are the best source for exact standards, permitted colours and height ranges. Studbook-related records are commonly maintained through organisations such as SA Studbook.

lessons.title: Assessing breed suitability for a purpose
lessons.html:
Start with the purpose

Choosing a horse begins with the job it must do, the rider or handler, the environment and the budget. A breed that excels in one purpose can be unsuitable or even dangerous in another.

Matching breeds to purposes

PurposeRequirementsCommonly suitable breeds
Flat racingSpeed, stride, heart and lung capacityThoroughbred
Endurance ridingStamina, efficient cooling, sound feet, recovery rateArabian and Arabian crosses, Boerperd
Show jumping and dressagePower, elasticity, trainability, sizeWarmbloods, Thoroughbreds, Thoroughbred crosses
Cattle work on farmsAgility, quick acceleration, calm, cow sense, hardinessQuarter Horse, Boerperd
Trail riding and tourism in rough terrainSure-footedness, calm temperament, hardiness, good feetBasuto pony, Nooitgedacht, Boerperd
Children's ridingSize, calm and reliable temperamentWell-schooled ponies (e.g. Welsh, Basuto, Nooitgedacht)
Draught and drivingStrength, calm, steady pullPercheron, Clydesdale, Friesian (lighter driving)

Factors beyond breed

  • Individual conformation and soundness: a poorly built member of a suitable breed may be less useful than a sound cross-bred.
  • Temperament and training: a highly-strung Thoroughbred off the track is rarely suitable for a novice rider without re-training.
  • Climate and management: hardy breeds cope with veld grazing and heat; fine-coated breeds need more feed, shelter and care. Consider local disease risks such as African horse sickness and the need for vaccination.
  • Cost: purchase price, feed requirements, shoeing and veterinary costs in rand, and resale value.
  • Rider: size, weight and experience.

Making an assessment

  1. Define the purpose and constraints in writing.
  2. List the traits needed and rank them.
  3. Compare candidate breeds against the traits, using breed standards.
  4. Assess individual horses for conformation, soundness (pre-purchase vet examination), temperament and training.
  5. Make a justified recommendation and record the reasons.

Example

A guest farm in the Drakensberg wants horses for novice trail riders on steep, rocky paths. Required traits: calm, sure-footed, hardy on veld grazing, sound feet, moderate size. A Basuto pony or Nooitgedacht type would usually suit better than a Thoroughbred, which would need more feed and care and may be too sensitive for novices.

Key points

  • Breeds developed through selection for work, climate and isolation.
  • Main categories: hot bloods, warmbloods, cold bloods, ponies, stock and gaited horses.
  • The Thoroughbred descends from three Eastern foundation sires; the Arabian from Bedouin breeding.
  • South African breeds include the Boerperd, Basuto pony and Nooitgedacht.
  • Assess suitability by purpose, then individual conformation, temperament, management and cost.
